China’s dominance of several aspects of the advanced energy technology market has left island nations increasingly dependent on China for these technologies and for supporting grid infrastructure upgrades. A number of U.S. allies are incorporating Chinese-built assets, such as solar PV systems and transformers, to bolster their energy resilience. For instance, Chinese-built solar technology filled the electricity gap left when Japan shut down its nuclear plants in the wake of the Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011 (Coca 2024). In another example, the Philippines is increasingly dependent on China for grid updates. China owns 40% of the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (Lema and Flores 2024), and the imminent depletion of the Malampaya gas source in the South China Sea, which supplies 20% of Luzon’s (the largest and most populous island in the Philippines) electricity (Malampaya 2024), will intensify dependence on imports. The large share of power grid and advanced energy components provided by China exacerbates uncertainty surrounding cyber vulnerabilities. In a contested environment, geographic constraints on energy transmission methods (e.g., limited overland infrastructure and the vulnerabilities of undersea cables to, for example, China’s newly unveiled deep-sea cable cutter [Chen 2025]) make local energy unlikely as a dependable DOW energy source. C.3 Operational and Logistics Considerations The vast distances between landmasses and from the U.S. mainland in the Pacific, combined with the need to disperse assets to counter Chinese surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting capabilities (Simulcik, Villalobos, and Bazilian 2025), underscore the need for power-dense, logistically flexible energy technologies to support USINDOPACOM operations. Lithium-ion batteries, though widely used in civilian sectors, bring added logistics considerations. Recall from Section 3.5 of this report that they offer only a fraction (15.3%) of the energy per volume compared to gasoline equivalents (AFDC 2024; Shaffer 2024). Similarly, solar and wind energy typically require significantly more surface area to generate comparable power (Van Zalk and Behrens 2018), making them less practical as stand-alone power sources for rapid deployment in space-constrained or contested environments. 64 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. DOW purchases nearly 50% of its fuel overseas from foreign partners (DOD 2023). Increased DOW reliance on advanced energy technologies (such as batteries) that are heavier and not as easy to store or transport over long distances compared to legacy fuels could pose risks in the vast USINDOPACOM region, where logistics are an ever-present challenge. Interoperability will face challenges in USINDOPACOM because, despite strong alliances and partnerships, there is no North Atlantic Treaty Organization-equivalent shared security pact that includes a majority of countries in the region. USINDOPACOM works with a wide range of allies and partners, each with their own standards and regulations. This variation can complicate the integration of energy technologies because each country might have different requirements and systems, and each country adopts advanced technologies at different rates.
